A model that predicts well can still be a black box. Explainability methods try to show which inputs a model relies on and how they change its predictions. This chapter covers three common ones, feature importance, partial dependence, and SHAP, and spends as much time on what they cannot tell you as on what they can, especially when the thing being explained is a spatial process.

::: {.callout-note title="Learning objectives"}
By the end of this chapter you should be able to

- compute and read feature importance, partial dependence, and SHAP values for a trained model
- explain what each method measures and how they differ
- say what these explanations can and cannot reveal about a spatial process
- explain why an explanation of a model is not the same as a causal explanation of the world
:::

## Feature importance

*To be written. Which features a model leans on most, and how that is measured.*

## Partial dependence

*To be written. How the prediction changes as one feature changes while the others are held fixed.*

## SHAP

*To be written. Splitting an individual prediction into contributions from each feature.*

## What explanations can and cannot say

*To be written. Explanations describe the model and not necessarily the world, and spatial data add problems of their own, such as features that are correlated with each other and with location.*
